findings.claim: The final scene is the most important in the play. Mickey discovers that Edward is his twin brother. Consumed by rage and envy (“I wish I was like him”), he confronts Edward at the Town Hall with a gun. The police arrive. Mickey is shot, and Edward also dies.
findings.truth: The order of events is inverted. Mrs Lyons tells Mickey that Linda and Edward have been seeing each other; Mickey takes Sammy's gun and confronts Edward at the Town Hall over the affair. Mrs Johnstone runs in and only then reveals that they are twins. Mickey accidentally fires the gun and kills Edward; the police then shoot Mickey. Lesson 1's own timeline gives the correct order, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Blood Brothers (musical)' plot; LitCharts plot summary (revelation order: affair, then twin revelation, then shooting)

findings.claim: The Beatles: References to The Beatles root the play firmly in Liverpool culture.
findings.truth: There is no Beatles reference in the play. The recurring cultural reference is Marilyn Monroe: the opening song is 'Marilyn Monroe', Russell reprises it in Act Two, and Mickey's dependence on pills is set against her story. (Russell wrote a separate early play about the Beatles, which is probably the source of the confusion.)
findings.evidence: Wikipedia song list for Blood Brothers (musical); Seneca / subplotter notes on the Marilyn Monroe motif

findings.claim: The Conservative government responded by withdrawing financial support for Liverpool rather than investing in it. (Repeated in the context match question: 'Thatcher's government withdrew financial support from Liverpool'.)
findings.truth: After the 1981 Toxteth riots the government sent Michael Heseltine to Merseyside as 'Minister for Merseyside'. He set up the Merseyside Task Force and launched the Liverpool International Garden Festival and the Mersey Basin Campaign. Treasury ministers argued privately for 'managed decline', but money was not publicly withdrawn.

findings.claim: Blood Brothers was written in 1981 and is set across the 1950s to the 1970s.
findings.truth: The play runs from the late 1950s to the early 1980s. Mickey's unemployment, the dole queue and the redundancies belong to the early-1980s recession, which is the period the same lesson teaches as the historical context.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Blood Brothers (musical)': spans the late 1950s to the early 1980s; Mickey faces unemployment in the early-1980s recession

findings.claim: Opening line: “Did you ever hear the story of the Johnstone twins?” (also set as the line to deliver in practice question 2)
findings.truth: The Narrator's opening line is “So did y'hear the story of the Johnstone twins? As like each other as two new pins...”
findings.evidence: GradeSaver Blood Brothers quotations page; StageAgent synopsis

findings.claim: Mickey's key line is “I wish I was like him.” (taught as a key quote in L2, L3, L7 and set as the line to deliver in L8 practice question 2)
findings.truth: No source gives that line. Mickey's line at the climax is “I could have been him!” (after 'Why didn't you give me away?'). The nearest other text is the lyric of 'That Guy': 'I wish that I could be like... that guy.' Students quoting the old wording would be quoting a line that is not in the text.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia and multiple study guides quote 'I could have been him!'; allmusicals lyric of 'That Guy'

findings.claim: You must mention these in every Section A answer. (playwright, genre, style)
findings.truth: The spec sets no such requirement. Section A is short-answer questions on the performance text and on the development of drama and performance, worth 50 marks and all AO3. A 4-mark costume question earns nothing for naming the playwright.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/drama-J316.md section 3a (Section A: short answer questions relating to the study of a text; 50 marks, AO3)

findings.claim: Apron — the area at the front of the stage that sticks out in front of the wings.
findings.truth: The apron is the part of the stage that extends in front of the proscenium arch. The wings are the offstage spaces at the sides.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Stage (theatre)': 'a stage may extend in front of the proscenium arch... This area is referred to as the apron'

findings.claim: In your OCR Drama exam... / In the OCR Drama exam... / In Section A of the OCR Drama exam...
findings.truth: House rule: student-facing text never names the exam board. Four lessons open by naming it.

findings.claim: Keeps distance from other characters (increased proximity).
findings.truth: Proximity means nearness, so 'increased proximity' means standing closer — the opposite of the point being made. A student writing this in an answer would describe the wrong staging.
findings.evidence: standard use of the term; the lesson's own earlier bullet uses 'close proximity' for standing close

findings.claim: Mrs Johnstone gives Edward a locket containing a photograph of herself.
findings.truth: The locket holds a photograph of Mrs Johnstone and Mickey. The picture of the other boy is what makes Mrs Lyons' reaction so violent.
findings.evidence: LitCharts plot summary: 'a locket with a picture of herself and Mickey'; Wikipedia plot

findings.claim: dole — Slang term for unemployment benefits (now called Jobseeker's Allowance), widely used in 1980s Britain.
findings.truth: Jobseeker's Allowance has largely been replaced by Universal Credit, so the parenthesis is out of date. Dropping it keeps the definition correct.
findings.evidence: UK benefits: income-based JSA replaced by Universal Credit

findings.claim: Quotations attributed to characters that could not be verified: Edward's “Do you want to be my friend?” (L2, L7, L8), “You're still my best friend”, “I don't care about money” (L2, L3), Mrs Johnstone's “I can't afford to keep both of them” (L2, L3 practice), “I'll always love you, Mickey”, “I had to give one away”, Mrs Lyons' “You swore on the Bible” (L2 practice), “I think you should go”, “You don't own him!”, “He's mine!”, Linda's “Leave him alone!”, “I love you, Mickey”, “You're not the Mickey I married”, Sammy's “Come on, Mickey, just do it”.
findings.truth: The play is in copyright and no script is on disk, so these could not be checked word for word. Two nearby lines that ARE verified: Mickey's first-meeting line is 'Do you wanna be my blood brother, Eddie?' and the final-scene line is 'Mickey. Don't shoot Eddie. He's your brother. You had a twin brother. I couldn't keep both you.' Recommend one pass against a copy of the script before the next cohort.
findings.evidence: GradeSaver quotations page; no source found for the other wordings

findings.claim: The CTPAPVE mnemonic (also in the lesson description).
findings.truth: The eight skills listed are Clarity, Tone, Pace, Pitch, Accent, Pause, Volume, Emphasis — CTPPAPVE, eight letters. The label has seven, so a student checking their recall against the acronym is one skill short. Tom's call, since it is a Unity mnemonic.

findings.claim: In traditional staging, Stage Right is associated with positive experiences and Stage Left with negative experiences.
findings.truth: There is no settled convention of this kind. What is generally agreed is that stage right reads as the 'stronger' position for audiences who read left to right. The design idea that follows (Lyons stage right, Johnstones stage left) still works without the claim about tradition.
findings.evidence: no authority found for a positive/negative convention

findings.claim: from the cramped streets of inner-city Liverpool to the leafy suburbs of Skelmersdale
findings.truth: Skelmersdale is a Lancashire new town built to rehouse Liverpool families, not a suburb of Liverpool. The same lesson calls it a new town further down.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Blood Brothers (musical)' (set in Liverpool and later Skelmersdale); Skelmersdale new town

findings.claim: a pulsating blue and red light ... to show that the police have arrived (repeated in L8: 'Blue and red pulsating strobes')
findings.truth: British police vehicles use blue lights; red is a North American convention. It is a designer's choice rather than a claim about the play, so it is left alone, but blue alone is the period-accurate signal.

findings.claim: Received Pronunciation ... sometimes called BBC English or the Queen's English.
findings.truth: Since September 2022 the usual form is the King's English. Not worth an edit on its own, but worth catching in the next sweep of the glossary and flashcard.

summary: Eight lessons checked against the OCR J316 spec and against verified plot and quotation sources. One HIGH finding: lesson 8 inverts the final scene, telling students Mickey learns he is Edward's twin before he confronts him. Also fixed: an invented Beatles reference, a wrong account of the response to the Toxteth riots, the play's date range, two misquoted 'key' lines, an exam claim the spec does not support, the apron definition, a proximity slip and the locket's contents. Four lessons named the exam board in student-facing prose and are de-branded. The remaining quoted lines could not be checked because the play is in copyright and no script is on disk.
